meta.title: Regex engines on every platform: ECMA-262 compliance and performance
meta.lede: How closely the regular expression engines of each platform follow ECMA-262, and how fast they are. Engines that implement ECMA-262 and each platform's other regex engines appear side by side, with V8 as the common reference, judged on the ECMA-262 test data and timed over the Industry workloads of dotnet/performance. Every engine ran on this runner tonight, in one job, so a figure compares across languages as well as within one.

meta.method:
What this page shows. The regular expression engines of each platform, side by side: engines that implement ECMA-262 (the regular expressions of JavaScript), the platform's other regex engines, which implement other dialects, and V8, the engine of Node.js and Chrome, as the common reference. Each engine is judged on the ECMA-262 test data, whose answers are V8's, and timed over the Industry workloads of dotnet/performance. An engine that does not implement ECMA-262 is there for its speed alone. How each engine is called is in the list of engines at the foot of the page.

A figure is the time to count every match a global search finds over the whole text of a workload, moving on one character after an empty match as JavaScript's matchAll does, in nanoseconds per count. An ECMA-262 engine is given the workload's flags with u, and V8 the flags with g and u. An engine of another dialect is given the pattern as it is with the workload's i, m and s flags, and has no figure where the pattern does not compile.

How it is measured. Every harness keeps to one protocol. The workloads run one after another, each in 3 rounds of every engine in turn, the order of the engines turned each round. Each turn is a process of its own, which warms the engine, times 7 passes of as many counts as fit in 0.7 s, and reports the median pass. An engine's figure for a workload is the median of its rounds, and its spread is the fastest and the slowest round; a figure whose spread is over 5% is listed in the facts. Work a program would do once per text, such as checking that bytes are UTF-8, is done before the timing starts.

Where the figures come from. This repository's nightly workflow runs each source's published container image, at its newest release, one after another in one job on one runner. Each image runs its engines and V8 over the workloads, then the ECMA-262 test data for compliance. So the figures of every engine run here were measured on one machine in one night's run. Anyone can add an engine: see implementing a source.

Compliance beside an engine's name is its result on the ECMA-262 test data: its right answers over every answer the data asks in the encodings the engine answers in, counted by the data's own rule (tools/answers.py), so that an answer its runner did not ask counts against it as a wrong one does. An engine with one encoding is a share of that encoding's answers, and says which. So is an engine that implements only some of the three grammars (u, v and the legacy one without either), and one with another version of Unicode than the data's (whose answers are V8's), which is judged by the answers of its version: the list of engines gives each engine's grammars and version. The counts are in its tooltip. Counts worked out at an earlier commit of the data (for an engine too slow to judge every night) are a share of what that commit asks, and say which commit. "Not ECMA-262" marks an engine that implements another dialect.

> 30 s in a cell: the engine did not produce a result within 30 s. Every harness stops a figure that has not finished in 30 s and does not run it again in the workload's later rounds, so such a cell has no figure, and the engine is not ranked on that workload.

≠ count in a cell: the engine's count of matches on that workload differs from V8's, which is a wrong answer. An ECMA-262 engine with one has no figure there, and is not shown as fully compliant beside its name whatever its share of the test data. An engine of another dialect keeps its figure, and the workload shows both counts. A cell marked failed says, in its tooltip, what the harness reported.

compliance.note: captures.jsonl is judged over UTF-16 only, since regress has no UTF-8 interface
judged over UTF-16 only, since libregexp has no UTF-8 interface; replace and split are the runner's, over its exec

Judged over UTF-16 only, through its exec (replace and split are the runner's), each worker in a child process, a record with no answer in 10 s counted unanswered. std::regex implements the ECMAScript grammar of ECMA-262's 3rd edition (1999), as the C++ standard modifies it: it has no u or v flag, so it is judged in the legacy grammar alone, and it has no lookbehind and no named groups, so those count against it there.

Judged over UTF-16 only, through its exec (replace and split are the runner's), each worker in a child process, a record with no answer in 10 s counted unanswered. SRELL always reads a pattern as the u flag does (and as the v flag does with unicodesets), so it is judged in those two grammars; its Unicode tables are 18.0, so it is judged by the data's answers for Unicode 18.0.
Over UTF-16 (ecma_utf16 texts) and UTF-8 (R's strings, and raw vectors for a text or pattern with a NUL).
